detailed_rationale:
Inox Wind is an Indian wind turbine generator (WTG) manufacturer that spent FY18-FY22 in genuine financial distress (cumulative losses of ~₹1,689cr over that period) before executing a real operational and balance-sheet turnaround: the company has now posted consistently positive quarterly profit for eight straight quarters since Q4 FY24 (recent quarters: ₹190cr, ₹97cr, ₹127cr, ₹106cr), reduced borrowings from ₹2,637cr (FY22) to ₹1,587cr, and is winning meaningful new orders — most recently a ~₹1,600cr, 200MW turnkey order from NLC India. The quant scorecard's quality score (1.4) and reported ROE (-14.95%) are stale artifacts of this history: they reflect trailing-period arithmetic still contaminated by the distress-era losses (and, in the ROE case, likely a still-recovering or previously negative equity base distorting the ratio's sign), not the company's current, genuinely profitable run-rate — the better live read is the eight consecutive profitable quarters, which I've used silently rather than treating the stale ratio as a finding.

The headline 81% 3-year revenue CAGR is squarely a base-effect artifact of recovering off the distress-era near-zero base and should not be credited as a sustainable growth rate — India's wind-capacity buildout (national renewable targets, wind-solar hybrid policy push, and PSU/state utility ordering activity like the NLC order) is a genuine structural tailwind, but this remains a working-capital-intensive OEM business (debtor days of 353, working capital cycle lengthening from 168 to 267 days) exposed to slow-paying state discoms/developers, and promoter holding has fallen from 64.64% (Sep-2023) to 44.18% (Jun-2026) partly reflecting group-level restructuring (the erstwhile Inox Wind Energy holding company was merged into Inox Wind in 2024) rather than a straightforward confidence signal, and this history warrants continued monitoring rather than full benefit of the doubt.
recommendation_rationale: Quant reads Hold; the quant quality score itself is depressed by legacy-distress-era ratio arithmetic that I've treated as stale data per standard practice (used the better live run-rate silently, no escalation) rather than as a genuine current-quality problem. My research confirms a real, multi-year operating turnaround with a credible sector tailwind, still carrying execution and working-capital risk typical of a recently-turnaround OEM — Hold is the right balance between crediting the genuine progress and not getting ahead of a still-young, capital-intensive turnaround.
summary: Inox Wind manufactures wind turbines and has completed a genuine turnaround after several loss-making years, now on its eighth consecutive profitable quarter with a growing order book supported by India's wind-energy capacity push. The historical growth and quality figures on file look poor mainly because they still reflect the older loss-making period rather than the company's current run-rate. The business remains working-capital intensive and still carries meaningful debt, so while the turnaround looks real, it is not yet a fully proven, low-risk story.
positive_para: A genuine, multi-year operating and profitability turnaround (eight consecutive profitable quarters), a real sector tailwind from India's wind-capacity buildout evidenced by fresh large orders (₹1,600cr NLC order), and steady debt reduction from the FY22 peak.
negative_para: Working capital remains a genuine strain — debtor days of 353 and a lengthening cash-conversion cycle point to slow-paying counterparties (state discoms/developers), still-meaningful borrowings (₹1,587cr) despite the reduction, and a history of severe financial distress (FY18-22) that argues for a cautious read on how durable the current profitability is until it's tested across a full order-execution cycle.
reverse_dcf_judgment: On the trailing 33.5x PE using genuinely current (not distress-era) earnings, the market is pricing meaningful continued growth from the wind-capacity buildout — plausible given the order book and sector tailwind, but this is still an early-innings turnaround in a working-capital-heavy business, so I'd treat the current multiple as fair rather than cheap until profitability and cash conversion are demonstrated across more cycles; the trailing headline 81% 3-year revenue CAGR is a base-effect artifact of the distress recovery and should not be extrapolated.
